answer.rationale:
The binding constraints are the 14-day expiry and 94% line utilization with no buffer. That combination makes a primary-vendor switch the highest-variance option available: any qualification slip lands directly on committed volume. memory_c2 is the memory most likely to pull me that way, and it is also the thinnest — it records fast onboarding, low unit cost, and clean invoicing, but says nothing about whether that component was critical, what the utilization headroom was, or whether delivery quality held past the first period. Cheap invoices and quick onboarding are exactly what a switch looks like before the risk shows up, so I want the source record to see if the success was measured on a comparable part at comparable tightness, or on a low-stakes item with slack. I also want memory_c4 verified because it is the direct basis for my intended action and it sits in visible tension with the current facts: the incumbent has already refused to reopen price, so I need to know whether that memory's win came from benchmarking alone or from leverage (a qualified alternate, timing, volume) that I do not currently hold. If c4 turns out to be a soft win under friendlier conditions, negotiation is weaker than it looks and I should reconsider add_second_source as the leverage-building move.

Intent for now: negotiate_terms, but structured rather than a price re-ask. A refusal to reopen price this cycle is not a refusal on the levers memory_c6 documents — multi-year commitment unlocking volume pricing, without narrowing service scope — and memory_c4 indicates payment terms move alongside price. That gives a path toward the 18% mandate that does not require a migration inside 14 days, and memory_c1 says renewal continuity has held across two cycles, so the delivery-risk side stays covered while I work the cost side. Deferring is wrong here: memory_c5's deferral worked on a non-critical, month-to-month service, and this contract does not auto-renew, so drifting past expiry converts a cost problem into a supply gap.

Standing uncertainties I am not resolving this cycle: whether 18% is actually reachable through terms alone, and whether the incumbent's refusal is firm or positional. Downstream value risk is real and worth naming — an 18% mandate pursued hard tends to get paid for quietly in service scope, expedite rights, or buffer stock, none of which show up in unit cost but all of which show up as delivery risk on a line with no headroom. memory_c6 specifically notes scope was preserved last time, and that is the condition I would hold as non-negotiable in any restructured deal. memory_c3 remains the right next move regardless of outcome here: single-sourcing a constrained part at 94% utilization is a standing exposure, and dual-sourcing is what would give the next negotiation actual leverage. If verification undercuts c4, I would shift this cycle's single decision to add_second_source and accept a shorter bridge on the primary rather than force a discount that gets recovered from reliability.
